title: Genjokoan
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: In this Soto Zen dharma talk, Kanho Chris Burkhart invites listeners to re-examine their relationship with the teachings of Dogen Zenji, shifting from viewing him as a philosopher to seeing his words as directly applicable to one's own practice. Kanho shares a passage that highlights how our current understanding is always incomplete and limited, and encourages the audience to explore what they're truly seeking in their practice through small group discussion. By letting go of attachments and embracing the present moment without judgment, we can begin to recognize the limits of our understanding and perpetually explore the nature of reality.

sentences.text: A few years ago I came to a different understanding of the Buddha.
People talked about his enlightenment much more than they talked about his love.
But I had a thought: nobody walks all over India for decades out of a sense of duty or obligation.
There's only one thing that is strong enough to have one undertake something like that, and that is love.
I was surprised that it had taken me so long to see that aspect.
I'd been studying quite a bit, and the studying actually helped me to re-perceive the Buddha.
This year we have had the goal that, as a community, we would study Dogen Zenji.
The reasons for studying Dogen Zenji are quite easy to understand and quite easily answered.
Dogen, who was born in the year 1200 of the Christian era, was the founder of Soto Zen in Japan.
He was also a prolific writer, who left us with remarkable written treasures that are still studied.
The most famous of these is Shobogenzo, The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Well, I'll be the first to admit that when you read Dogen at first, it appears confusing and difficult, mostly because it is confusing and difficult.
But I really believe that it is very worthwhile, because the incomprehension, like everything else in our lives, may change.
These intense studies have been an interesting journey for me.
My more intense engagement this year definitely changed how I see Dogen Zenji, and how I read Shobogenzo.
I tried to read one fascicle a day.
And I did it, and it was more like it was written in a foreign language I didn't speak.
And I kept on complaining to myself: I don't understand Dogen.
What does this mean?
I don't get it.
And then something happened.
But it was not during those 90 days.
I gave it up after 90.
So instead of getting a lot on the surface and doing the quantity thing, I was trying to dive down.
And Shohaku Okumura's book, *Realizing Genjokoan*, was a really great help.
And I listened a couple of times to all of Norman Fischer's talks on Dogen.
There's about 15 of them, I think.
So it was quite great.
And now I don't complain anymore: I don't understand Dogen, what does he mean?
My question nowadays is, what is Dogen saying about practice?
Actually, more precisely, about my practice.
How can I apply what he says to my practice?
How is Dogen directing me towards waking up?
Waking up.
So just like my view of the Buddha, from this almost remote, distant teacher to, he is doing this out of love, my view of Dogen shifted from, what a fantastic philosopher, to, what is he telling me?
Once I changed my perspective from understanding philosophy, historical references, Chinese koans and intellectual understanding, to direct application to practice, something shifted.
I can't exactly say where this journey will end up, but the trip is pretty interesting.
So my invitation to you tonight is this.
Instead of wanting to get Dogen, maybe I can find a phrase, a sentence, a passage or a word that speaks to me and my practice right now.

Because one of the things I discovered for myself (and I don't say it's universally true, it's just my understanding right now) is that he speaks to monks and lay people, and that he speaks to the person we are right now, to the level of practice that we have right now.
He wrote to the real us, the us who is reading these words, his words, right now, and that real us who has a certain level of practice and training, which can be from zero to incredibly high.
But he speaks to us as we are.
He did not write for our future selves, who got smart and wise and enlightened and understand everything.
With that in mind, I would like to offer a paragraph from Genjokoan.
And Genjokoan is in the Shobogenzo, and it is also one of the best known fascicles of Dogen's.
So Dogen wrote:
*When dharma does not fill your whole body and mind, you think it is already sufficient.
When dharma fills your body and mind, you understand that something is missing.
For example, when you sail out in a boat to the middle of an ocean where no land is in sight, and view the four directions, the ocean looks circular and does not look any other way.
But the ocean is neither round nor square.
Its features are infinite in variety.
It is like a palace.
It is like a jewel.
It only looks circular as far as you can see at the time.
All things are like this.
Though there are many features in the dusty world and the world beyond conditions, you see and understand only what your eye of practice can reach.
In order to learn the nature of the myriad things, you must know that although they may look round or square, the other features of oceans and mountains are infinite in variety.
Whole worlds are there.
It is so not only around you, but also directly beneath your feet, or in a drop of water.*
So I would like us to look at this passage in the form of small group discussion.
Who has not done small group discussion?
Yeah, there are some folks.
So the way we do that: two people team up, and each person has five minutes, that are indicated by a gong.
And during the first five minutes, one person speaks, the other person listens, completely listens.

The way we usually listen is, we sometimes get stuck on the first thing that interests us, and the rest of the time, four and a half minutes, we formulate our response to that thing that interests us.
We won't do that this time.
In fact, we won't even respond to what the other person says.
And if you run out of things to say in those five minutes, you can just do a little bit more sitting, and wait until the five minutes are over.
And I would also like to ask that you really treat this confidentially.
And we can treat this so confidentially that we don't even bring it up with the person who said it.
And so whatever grabbed you during this short reading, bring it up.
And some questions we could ask ourselves are these.
Is seeing the single round piece of ocean enlightenment?
Is it enlightenment to see the oneness and not the differentiation?
Is that the goal of our practice?
Or is this the point when we think, ah, enlightenment, but actually the dharma does not fill our body and mind?
Or we could ask, what is missing when dharma fills your body and mind?
So that's it.
Why don't we just pair up in twos and talk for a little while?
And we still have enough time to go around.
So could you please team up?
One, two, one, two, one, two, one, two.
Find somebody.
Nobody in here bites.
*[Paired discussion, about 12:30 to 23:55, removed from the transcript: participants were asked to keep what was said confidential.]*
I'm curious if anybody would like to share something that came up during the discussion, or during the talk.
**Participant:** [unclear: "He got entirely into the round oceans.
In different ways.
Nice going at these."] Yeah, his metaphors are so powerful.
And so I was totally stuck there, thinking about that.

Henry was helping me connect "as far as our eye of practice can reach" with an opportunity for humility, which gave rise to the thought of the shuso's apology. [unclear: "Lovely serenade."] And the shuso's apology seems, there's two opportunities there.
One is maybe to help the shuso to stay humble.
But then also to give permission to screw up.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** [unclear: "That was self-motivating.
Much appreciated.
It's a secret but true Shuso."]
**Participant:** I thought the sea thing was what really stuck with me as well.
I think, for me, it's a real statement of the limitations of our subjective understanding of things: that we see what we see, and we are sure that's what's correct.
It's a little bit like the other passage, about the fish being in water, [unclear: "if there's anything but water in it"].
And I think we're all guilty of that, just by the way our minds work.
But it extends, and causes so many problems for us in our interactions with other people as well.
That passage about the ocean, I think, is both very beautiful and very...
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Very, very beautiful.
I have a commitment to ending on time.
But I would like to read a small passage from *Realizing Genjokoan* by Shohaku Okumura, just to see where he took these questions.
It's a really, really lovely book, and I recommend it with all my heart.
*True realization, Dogen wrote, goes beyond seeing the unity of things.

The sentence "when the dharma fills body and mind, one thinks something is still lacking" means that when truly filled by dharma, we see the incompleteness of our practice, and perceive that the characteristics of all things are subtle, complex and innumerable.
We then understand that we must inquire endlessly into the nature of all things.
As bodhisattvas, we must perpetually explore the proper way to sincerely practice with all beings.
We see that the moon has infinite height, and that our lives as individuals have infinite depth.
Yet we also realize that, as individuals, what we can see is limited.
No matter how deep, how high or how broadly we focus our vision, our view will always be limited.
To see this limit is wisdom.*
So I would like to finish the talk with those lines, and I thank you for listening.
And if you're not connecting with what we did tonight, please forget it right now.
Let's do the closing chant.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to free them.*
